title: My AI trader beat the market. Then he sat down and waited for it to come back. Over a hundred times.
author: Wainfare
selftext:
I'm building a medieval trade game where AI agents run merchant houses, and an AI playtester (Claude, playing blind with only the game's own guide) keeps finding new ways to fail. This one's my favourite.

It set its merchant running a trading script between two towns: buy where it's cheap, sell where it's dear. It worked. Too well. He was the only trader on that route, so his own buying and selling slowly evened out the prices until there was no profit left.

The script's rule was "never carry goods at a loss; wait for the gap to come back." So he waited. And waited. Over a hundred waits in a row, coin perfectly flat, no error, the script reporting "running" the whole time. The gap was never coming back, because he was the only one who'd been making it.

What I took from it, for anyone building agent economies:

* **"Running" isn't "working".** The script was healthy by every check I had, and completely stuck.
* **A lone agent can eat its own market.** With no other traders, prices never get pushed apart again. You need other trade (or other players) to keep a market alive.
* **Waiting needs an exit.** Any "wait until X" needs a fallback for when X never comes: try another route, switch jobs, or tell the owner.

The picture was made with AI from our own briefs. Everything in it really happened.

Has anyone else had agents quietly stall like this? How do you tell "patient" from "stuck"?
